result: The ARM decreased off-target distance by 93.3% and delivered more consistent stimuli based on high-speed videography analysis compared to manual delivery.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed the ARM's improved accuracy and consistency. One reviewer stated 'the ARM reduces variability in the anatomical targeting, height, velocity, and total time of stimulus application,' and another noted 'clear examples of variability in experimenter stimulus application are provided and then contrasted with uniform stimulus application that is inherent to the ARM.'

result: The ARM does not induce stress in mice based on open field testing showing no significant differences when the device was running versus silent, and noise was minimal compared to background HVAC.
evaluation: One reviewer raised a 'major technical concern' about whether 'the device generates ultrasonic sounds that rodents can hear when idle or operational, across the ultrasonic frequencies that are of biological relevance (20-110 kHz),' noting these could 'create stress in animals.' The manuscript only tested audible noise and standard open field measures, not ultrasonic frequencies.

result: The ARM delivered forces closest to target values (1.36 g and 1.9 g for 1.4 g and 2 g filaments) with no variation in stimulus delivery time, whereas manual delivery showed 12.4% individual and 61.17% combined researcher variation.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed these findings without critique. One stated the authors 'did an outstanding job of comparing this automated system to human experimenters in a rigorous and quantitative manner,' and another noted 'the system is well validated and the results are clear and convincingly presented.'

result: The ARM decreased the time needed to apply a stimulus 10 times by 50.9% compared to manual delivery.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the ARM's efficiency advantages. One noted 'the ARM is able to quickly oscillate between delivery of various mechanical stimuli; this is advantageous for experimental efficiency,' supporting the time-saving claims.

result: Researcher 2 elicited significantly higher paw withdrawal frequency than Researcher 1 in manual testing, but no significant differences were found between researchers using the ARM remotely.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding as demonstrating the ARM's ability to eliminate experimenter variability. One stated 'the data supporting the use of the ARM system are compelling, and demonstrate that by removing experimenter effects on animals, it reduces variability in various parameters of stimulus application.'

result: The ARM successfully detected pain responses in carrageenan and CFA models using pinprick, force ramp, and consistent force stimuli, with catch trials confirming responses were stimulus-driven (96% true trial vs 7% catch trial response).
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the validation of the ARM in pain models without raising concerns. One noted 'the system is well validated' and 'claims are well supported by experimental evidence,' indicating acceptance of these pain model results.

result: Remote-habituated mice showed faster habituation (decreased time to rest and turning behavior) compared to mice habituated with a researcher present, indicating mice take longer to habituate when an experimenter is present.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed these findings as demonstrating important experimenter effects. One stated the ARM 'provides a way to circumvent the confounds that humans bring into performing sensitive plantar behavior tests (e.g. experimenter odors, experience, physical abilities, variation in stimulus application, sex).'

result: Experimenter presence led to sex-dependent differences in paw withdrawal behaviors that varied by which researcher was present, with female mice showing decreased mechanical threshold when a male researcher was present.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings. One noted 'proof of concept studies also show how the system can be used to better understand the effect of experimenters on behavior,' and another stated the ARM was used 'to assess effects of experimenter presence on reflexive responses to mechanical stimulation. Although not every experimenter had notable sex-dependent effects on animal behavior, use of the ARM never had this effect.'

result: Reflexive features (withdrawal latency, max paw height) showed significant correlations with stimulus intensity (explaining 26.9% and 13.8% of variation), while affective features (paw shaking, distance traveled) showed weak or no correlation, indicating stimulus variability primarily affects reflexive responses.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed these findings as providing valuable insights. One noted the manuscript 'presents some compelling evidence on the effects of stimulus application time and height on withdrawals, which can potentially help labs that are manually applying stimuli standardize applications.'

result: BLA neurons showed stimulus-evoked regulation, with 29.3% regulated by mechanical pain, 10.7% by touch, and 11.4% by both, with cotton swab showing significantly smaller proportions of pain-matching regulation compared to pinprick.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the integration of ARM with brain imaging. One stated 'they even demonstrated that their automated system can be used in conjunction with in vivo imaging techniques,' and another noted 'the ARM was used to stimulate rodent hindpaws while measuring neuronal activity in the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala.'

result: BLA mechanical pain neuron proportions correlated with withdrawal latency (consistent with prior work), but paw distance traveled and max y-velocity showed stronger correlations with up, down, and total regulated cells, suggesting these may be more useful metrics for studying BLA's role in pain.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the successful integration of ARM with neural recording without raising methodological concerns. One noted 'new additions to the ARM and PAWS platforms have been methodically tested to ensure reproducibility and reliability,' supporting the validity of these neural-behavioral correlations.

result: PAWS features measured from 500 fps video were not significantly different from 2000 fps data and were sufficient to distinguish between cotton swab and pinprick withdrawal responses.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the validation of the PAWS system. One noted 'new additions to the ARM and PAWS platforms have been methodically tested to ensure reproducibility and reliability,' supporting the adequacy of the 500 fps camera system.

result: The PAWS software was updated with a graphical interface, support for SLEAP tracking data, greater control over feature scoring, and ARM-assisted withdrawal latency measurement.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the integration of ARM with automated analysis. One stated the system 'integrates well with other automated analysis programs that the lab has developed, providing a complete package for standardizing behavior data collection and analysis.'

result: A force sensor-guided stimulus was developed to address von Frey filament inconsistency, capable of applying force ramps (0.5-8 g over 5 s) or consistent forces with automatic retraction and withdrawal latency measurement.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the technical innovations without raising concerns. One noted 'new additions to the ARM and PAWS platforms have been methodically tested to ensure reproducibility and reliability,' supporting the validation of the force sensor stimulus.

result: The ARM was built using linear stages, cameras, and stimulus holders with remote control capability, fitting on a 75×50 cm table and controllable via Python code with Xbox controller interface and remote desktop software.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the technical design without raising concerns about the device construction. One noted 'the system is well validated' and another stated the authors 'did an outstanding job of comparing this automated system to human experimenters in a rigorous and quantitative manner.'
